About: The Impulse–Momentum Theorem

Source

Topic
Newtonian mechanics — impulse and momentum
Concept
The impulse delivered by a collision is fixed by the momentum change alone; contact time trades off against average force in exact inverse proportion.
Star control
Contact time — sweep from 0.01 s to 0.20 s while the shaded area (impulse) stays constant.
Misconception targeted
"A softer catch reduces the momentum change." It does not — the same impulse is spread over more time.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The setup

A cricket ball flies in at 30 m/s and rebounds at 20 m/s off a padded wall. Press ▶ to watch one collision; the shaded rectangle is the contact force.

Compared to just stopping it, what does the rebound do to Δp? (Incoming is +x.)

2 · Predict: stretch the contact

You now raise the contact time from 0.01 s to 0.20 s — a 20× stretch — keeping the mass and both speeds fixed. Δp cannot change (it is set by the velocities alone).

What happens to the average force F̄ during contact?

3 · Sweep it and watch

Now drag the Contact time slider all the way to 0.20 s. Watch the F–t rectangle: it goes short and wide. Height falls with 1/Δt while width grows with Δt, so the shaded area — the impulse — stays the same. The average-force readout falls by a factor of twenty; the impulse readout does not budge.

The wall pad also visibly compresses further for longer contacts — the softness is what BUYS the extra time.

4 · The cricket fielder

A fielder catches a ball travelling at u. Their hands, drawn back on impact, stretch the contact from a few milliseconds (rigid catch) to a tenth of a second or more.

The ball's Δp = m·u is fixed by the catch itself. What the drawn-back hands do is spread the same impulse over more time, dropping the average force by an order of magnitude — and the sting with it. Same argument: crumple zones, airbags, boxing gloves, landing with bent knees.

5 · Catch vs bounce

Try the extreme case: set rebound speed = 0. The ball is caught, not bounced. Now Δp = m·u = 4.5 N·s — smaller than the 7.5 N·s of the bounce, because the bounce has to both STOP and REVERSE the motion.

A bounce costs more impulse than a catch. This is why a ball hitting a hard wall recoils harder than one landing in a glove — and why, in Newton's cradle, the transferred impulse is doubled compared to a sticky collision.

01

At a glance

A ball flies into a padded wall and comes back off it, while a graph records the force the wall puts on the ball during the touch. You choose the ball's mass, how fast it arrives and leaves, and how long the contact lasts.

What you'll learn

  • What impulse is, and how to read it from a force–time graph.
  • How the ball's mass and speeds fix its change in momentum.
  • How contact time and average force are linked, and why that matters for catches and crashes.
The ball arrives with speed u. The graph on the right is where the sim draws the contact force.

What's on screen

  • Ball and pad: the ball with an arrow showing its velocity, a pad that gets thicker and softer as the contact time grows, and a label for the phase: incoming, contact, rebound or caught.
  • Force–time graph: a red shaded rectangle for the contact. Its width is the contact time Δt and its height is the average force.
  • Readings (sidebar): the impulse |J| and the average force |F̄|, as sizes.
See itRun the opening collision. Watch for: the ball arriving, pressing into the pad, and leaving, with a red rectangle on the graph below.

03

Impulse is the area under the force–time graph

A force acting for a time delivers an impulse. For a force that changes, it is the area under the force–time graph. The sim shows the contact as one rectangle at the average force F̄:

J = ∫F dt = F̄ Δt = Δp
Impulse equals the change in momentum, Δp = m(vf − vi).

The last equality is the impulse–momentum theorem. It follows from Newton's second law, F = dp/dt, added up over the contact. It holds whatever the shape of the force pulse, so an average force is enough to find Δp.

With F̄ = 750 N acting for Δt = 0.010 s the area is 7.5 N·s, and the sim prints |J| beside the rectangle. A real contact force rises and falls, so its peak is higher than F̄.

See itSet the contact time to 0.050 s. Watch for: |F̄| = 150 N and |J| = 7.50 N·s, a rectangle 0.05 s wide with 150 N × 0.05 s = 7.5 N·s.
04

A rebound changes momentum by m(u + w)

Take +x along the incoming motion. Before the contact the ball's momentum is +mu. After it, the ball moves back with speed w, so its momentum is −mw.

Δp = −mw − mu = −m(u + w)
The size is |Δp| = m(u + w); the minus sign means the push on the ball points along −x.
  • Catch (w = 0): the wall only removes mu.
  • Rebound: the wall removes mu, then gives the ball mw the other way.

For 0.15 kg at u = 30 m/s and w = 20 m/s, |Δp| = 0.15 × 50 = 7.5 N·s. A catch of the same ball gives 0.15 × 30 = 4.5 N·s. The graph hangs below its zero line because the force on the ball points along −x, and the readings show sizes only.

See itCatch the ball by setting w = 0. Watch for: the ball staying on the pad, and |J| reading 4.50 N·s instead of the 7.50 N·s of the rebound.
05

The same impulse over a longer time means a smaller force

The contact time Δt does not appear in Δp = m(vf − vi), so changing it leaves the impulse alone. Only the average force has to change:

F̄ = Δp / Δt, so F̄ ∝ 1/Δt
At fixed m, u and w: twice the time, half the average force.

Opening values give Δp = 7.5 N·s:

Δtaverage force |F̄|impulse |J|
0.010 s750 N7.5 N·s
0.050 s150 N7.5 N·s
0.200 s37.5 N7.5 N·s

Δt grows 20 times, so F̄ shrinks 20 times. On the graph the rectangle gets wider and lower while its area stays at 7.5 N·s.

See itStretch the contact to 0.200 s. Watch for: |F̄| falling to about 38 N while |J| stays at 7.50 N·s, and the rectangle running wide and flat.
06

Where it matters

  • Cricket catch. A fielder draws the hands back. The ball's Δp = mu is fixed, so a longer stop means a smaller average force on the hands.
  • Airbags and crumple zones. They stretch the time over which a person's momentum drops to zero, which cuts the average force.
  • Bent knees on landing. Bending adds time to the stop, so the legs and joints feel a smaller force than with a stiff landing.
  • Bounce versus catch. A ball that rebounds from a wall changes momentum by more than one that is caught, so it takes a larger impulse.
Go deeper: the sim's two independent sliders

In the sim, w and Δt are separate sliders so that each effect can be seen alone. For a real ball and surface they are linked: a stiff, bouncy pad tends to give a short contact and a high rebound. The theorem holds either way.

07

Summary

In one line. The force a wall exerts on a ball, added up over the time of contact, equals the ball's change in momentum.

Key points

  • Impulse J = ∫F dt = F̄ Δt is the area under the force–time graph, and J = Δp.
  • A rebound gives |Δp| = m(u + w); a catch gives mu.
  • At fixed Δp, the average force goes as 1/Δt.

Common mix-ups

  • "A softer catch reduces the momentum change." It does not. Δp is set by the speeds alone. The softness only spreads the same impulse over more time.
  • "A bounce is a catch in reverse, so Δp is the same." The wall must also send the ball back, so the change in momentum is larger than for a catch.
  • "The force on the ball is positive because the ball moves in +x." The force comes from the wall and points along −x, opposing the incoming motion.

Things to try on your own

  • Set w = 0 and Δt = 0.050 s. Predict |J| and |F̄| from m and u, then check the readings.
  • Find a pair of values of u and w that give |J| = 10.5 N·s with m = 0.15 kg.
  • Choose m, u and w so that the impulse is 15 N·s, then find the Δt that keeps |F̄| below 500 N.
